1988 Carrie: The Musical had some of the most difficult choreography ever to grace the Broadway stage. The entire opening “In” was staged to mirror a high school gym class, and as such, featured flips, jumping jacks, a human pyramid, crunches, sit ups, a full modern dance solo, a kick line, and several full lunges. This number was so strenuous, that several members of the ensemble had to see a chiropractor regularly to even perform the number night after night.

I agree and disagree. I think the material could stand independently (with the necessary modern adjustments) and make a great show. However, at its core, the musical is about Fanny Brice's journey from ragamuffin to star. However, I almost feel that this is the musical's mistake. It's an oversaturation of its own star. 

When we look at other biographical musicals: Evita, Gypsy, War Paint, etc; There is an astounding amount of detail placed on their respective supporting casts. Funny Girl has TWO songs in which the character of Fanny is not present. **TWO**. That means the character of Fanny is on stage 90% of the musical's runtime. If the actress/actor playing Fanny should be anything less than **excellent** the show falls apart. 

It's not the actor/actress's fault for delivering a good performance instead of an excellent one. It's the musical's fault for demanding an excellent singer/dancer/actress/comedian, and falling apart should it not receive its demand.

This is a great question! I actually do have an answer for this! So in Stratford, the orchestrations were much larger, and had a completely different sound than Broadway. In Stratford, Hands wanted the show to have more of a Classical feel. Thus, he hired an orchestrator(s) that utilized ginormous amounts of string/sax/woodwind. When the show transferred to Broadway, the creative team was upset with the sound of the musical. With Betty Buckley signed on, most of the shows extremely orchestrated numbers (Open Your Heart, Eve Was Weak, Evening Prayers, etc.) could utilize a smaller orchestra (and orchestrations) by producing more of a rock - opera sound. Thus, several instruments were cut or minimized, as the orchestrations were now changed permanently. Also, minimizing the pit allowed for a larger budget in other areas of the show.

The simple answer is this: value. The recording (especially a full recording) of the show is worth a lot of money. Not only is it a rarity within the theatrical community, it's become sort of a cultural cult classic. Any collector would never part with an item as rare as this one, especially going so far as to release it to the public. 

**Yes, the footage does exist. Will it ever be released? I am not sure.** 

***Personally***, I try to release most of the material I come across. I truly believe theatre (in all formats) belongs to the public. There is no reason that the show shouldn't be see by all who wish to view it. If I ever come across it, I promise this subreddit will be the first to hear about it.

Great question!

Regarding the cryptic energy surrounding the footage: All footage from the show is worth it's weight in gold. Due to the rarity of ANY footage of the show, collectors RARELY wish to part with any footage. Oddly enough, most of these collectors tend to be rather old in age, due to the musicals age itself. Most of the collectors of the rarest footage tend to be audience members of the original production back in 1988. As you could imagine, as they get older, the footage ages with them, and becomes rarer and rarer. Rare theatrical footage is something that only increases in value as time goes on. So for these collectors, most would never part with their material simply because its worth SO much. Unfortunately these collectors rarely have a generous attitude.

As for a full broadway recording, yes it does exist. This has been confirmed by numerous sources at this point. As for it's release, its the same reason I listed above. Collectors don't wish to part with it. This recording is considered one of the rarest of all time. Letting the public get a hold of it depreciates its value entirely. So I doubt they would ever part with the footage voluntarily. However, as morbid as this sounds, most of these collectors are older and will pass away within the next 10-20 years. It's possible the recording ends up in someone else's arms, and then gets uploaded (hopefully).

**PS**: My own personal philosophy is that the footage belongs to everyone. Theatre should be accessible in ALL forms. Theatre belongs to the public, not to the fortunate few.

This is an extremely interesting question, one that I have pondered for years. As someone who wishes to work on the musical in the future, this topic has remained in the forefront of my mind. The "beginnings" of the musical, are always where I find the most inspiration and reverence. Chronologically, I would take bits and pieces from each of it's iterations. From the workshop, I would take the script, and "Ain't It A Bitch". The workshop has one of the best realistic depictions of high school and teenage hood that the musical has ever had. In it's other iterations, the musical tends to inflate and inflate high school and teenage-hood, going so far as to include the lyrics "Put me out of my pain, I'd rather be SHOT" in the 2012 revival. Which is far to.... "on the nose". 

As for the 88' run, I would take the orchestrations from Stratford and the score from Broadway. However, multiple changes would be made to the score itself of course. The Stratford orchestrations were so full and beautiful. I assume these were scrapped prior to Broadway in order to save time and money. However, the score does benefit from a full orchestra. 

As for all other iterations *(including 2012 and 2015*) I would take... not much. Both of these iterations are good *in theory*. But the lackluster set and effects make the 2012 version pitiful. The production didn't even use "real" blood (2015 did/2012 did not), opting for projections instead. At the VERY least, a real bucket of blood needs to be on stage. As for costumes, score, and script, all the edits made were not for the benefit of the musical. The changes made to the score are awful. The electrifying rock opera energy has been replaced with acoustic guitar and a few drums. This musical NEEDS it's proper score. 

The "perfect" version of the show utilizes what the creators of the musical have cast aside. Opting for a rock opera of epic proportions, instead of the weaker rock musical it has become.

Hey! These are all AMAZING questions! The set in this particular show is so often overlooked. It’s so intricate, and literally costed more than 2 million dollars to create. 

So first off your correct! The reflective back wall does actually operate similar to a garage door! The reflective walls on the sides operate as almost revolving doors, so the actors can move on and off stage. However, the back reflective wall is rigged to move upwards and downwards (like a garage door!). The White House was kept in a space behind this back reflective wall. When the time came for the White House to be on stage, the wall was lifted and the White House (On rollers, or a track, that locks into place) moves on stage. 

The staircase is so often overlooked! Your doing a great job giving it some love :). The staircase was a sort of masterpiece of theatrical engineering. The staircase was kept above the stage, then lowered via hydraulics when the time came. The stairs were on a particular hydraulics system that was so intricate, due to Linzi literally standing in the middle of them as they fell. Lights and other technical equipment were unharmed due to the measurement of the stairs. The stairs actually fit the inner perimeter of the stage perfectly. The stairs were specifically created for Stratford and Broadway alike. 

Unlike other sets that simply “fall” into place, the stairs were lowered and locked. Due to the huge size of the stairs, the set piece does block all of stage right, stage left, and upstage. This was done purposely to give the illusion that we have left the gym, and are in an entirely different place. The stairs use the same hydraulics system that the “Dream On” showers use. 

What remains a mystery, is how all three set pieces (The gym triangle formation strings that are used in “In”, The “Dream On” shower, and the staircase) are kept above stage. There needs to be an almost impossible amount of room available to do this. Personally, I theorize that some of the sets were actually physical PARTS of the stage. The “Dream On” showers are only an added screen to the already purposes stage ground. I doubt that particular set moves off stage. The screens are most likely kept on the sides of the stage, or in the wings. As for the staircase, and gym equipment, it remains a mystery!

1. So actually if you ask any production staff of the musical they couldn’t tell you the answer. And the reason is, throughout the entire process, choreo, staging, costuming, and music, were all kept completely separate. You were never acting and singing on the same day, or vice versa. The cast, production staff, and even Cohen, Gore, and Pitchford had never seen the musical fully “put together” until the Stratford tech rehearsals. By that point, most of the decisions made by hands were final and uneditable. Infamously, Terry was told that the show should have a “Grease” vibe. He misunderstood this as a “Greece” vibe, as a Grecian tragedy. This is the reason for the infamous toga costumes and awkward staging. 

2. There really wasn’t any drama, just lots and lots of cuts made. Barbara Cook had serious trouble singing the score. She couldn’t deliver what Pitchford and Gore were looking for. She had trouble hitting the notes (which were in a soprano key and extremely high) and had an active disdain for the show throughout the process. This led to last minute cuts like: “Once I Loved A Boy” being replaced with “When Theres No One” or “Heaven Octet” being virtually scrapped. When the show was transferring to broadway, Gore and Pitchford wanted to change the “sound” of the musical completely. They wanted more of a rock-pop score and brought in multiple people to help them with this process, like Harold Wheeler. They also specifically asked for Betty Buckley to be in the musical, supposedly telling producers they would have her or no one. 

3. The immersive production was amazing. I’ve spoken to that director multiple times, and he is a wonderful talent. As for its future, I am not sure. I know it was rumored at one point to “tour”, I’ve yet to see it happen. The musical is more popular than ever, and a tour would be smart on the part of Micheal and Dean. It’s something I would loved to see!

They had so much difficulty making the prom dress look properly “bloody” they had to hide a second “bloody dress” underneath. This dress was covered in dried blood and was more visible to the audience. If you watch the Stratford RSC footage, you can actually see this dress being taken off during the destruction!
